name: Motixafortide
evidenceNote: Approved by the FDA in September 2023 on the strength of GENESIS, a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial in 122 people with multiple myeloma.
summary: Motixafortide (Aphexda) is an injected peptide that releases stem cells from bone marrow so they can be collected for transplant in multiple myeloma.
keyTakeaway: Motixafortide is a synthetic cyclic peptide that blocks CXCR4, the receptor that anchors blood-forming stem cells in bone marrow. Given once with the growth factor filgrastim, it pushes those cells into the bloodstream so they can be harvested before an autologous (own-cell) transplant. In the GENESIS trial, 67.5% of myeloma patients reached the collection target in up to two sessions after one dose, versus 9.5% on placebo. The FDA approved it as Aphexda in 2023. Allergic reactions, including rare anaphylactic shock, require premedication.

blocks.text: Motixafortide is a synthetic peptide of 14 amino acids, several of them unusual building blocks such as citrulline and naphthylalanine, closed into a ring by a disulfide bond. It is sold as Aphexda, a powder that is dissolved and injected under the skin [1].

It has one job: helping people with multiple myeloma, a cancer of plasma cells in the bone marrow, give up enough of their own blood-forming stem cells for a transplant. An autologous stem cell transplant, using the patient's own stored cells, improves survival in myeloma, but many people cannot collect enough cells when a growth factor injection is used alone [2].

Stem cells stay in the marrow partly because of a molecular tether. A chemokine called SDF-1 alpha (also known as CXCL12) binds the CXCR4 receptor on stem cells, guiding them home to the marrow and helping hold them to the surrounding matrix [1].

Motixafortide occupies CXCR4 and blocks SDF-1 alpha from binding. With the tether released, stem and progenitor cells spill into the circulating blood, where an apheresis machine can filter them out. White blood cell counts rise at the same time, an effect seen in mice, rats, dogs, and people [1].

It is paired with filgrastim (G-CSF), a growth factor that boosts stem cell production over several days. Filgrastim fills the marrow; motixafortide opens the door. The GENESIS investigators described it as having extended activity in the body, and reported that it preferentially mobilized more primitive stem cells [2].

Yes. The FDA approved Aphexda (NDA 217159) on September 8, 2023, and approved a supplement to the application in March 2026 [3]. The label limits its use to mobilizing stem cells, together with filgrastim, for collection and later autologous transplantation in patients with multiple myeloma [1].

blocks.text: It is used in transplant centers for adults with multiple myeloma who are preparing for an autologous stem cell transplant. In the trial and on the label, patients first receive filgrastim daily for four days; motixafortide is then injected the evening before the first collection, with a second dose possible before a third collection if the target has not been met [1].

GENESIS enrolled 122 patients at 18 sites in five countries and randomized them 2 to 1 to motixafortide or placebo, both with filgrastim. The goal was to collect at least 6 million CD34+ cells (a marker of stem cells) per kilogram of body weight [2]. The median age was 63, and 70% had already been treated with lenalidomide, a common myeloma drug [1].

rows: Target reached in up to 2 collections
Minimum of 2 million cells/kg in 1 collection

blocks.text: The published paper reports higher figures, 92.5% versus 26.2% for the primary goal [2]; the label's numbers come from a central-laboratory analysis limited to a single dose [1]. Both analyses point the same way. Time to blood count recovery after transplant and the durability of the graft were similar between groups [1].

The most serious risk is anaphylactic shock, which occurred in 0.7% of 407 patients across clinical studies, within 5 to 30 minutes of the dose. Hypersensitivity reactions affected 7.6% of patients in GENESIS. The label calls for premedication before every dose with an antihistamine, an acid-reducing H2 blocker, and a leukotriene blocker, plus a pain reliever for injection site reactions, and for dosing only where emergency treatment is available [1].

Other warnings: it may mobilize leukemia cells and should not be used in leukemia; it raises white blood cell counts, which need monitoring; tumor cells could be released from the marrow and collected with the graft, with unknown consequences; and it can harm a developing fetus [1].
